name: Bakairi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 further work read, von den Steinen 1892 (p. 320 'Accent'), also discusses stress and agrees on the penultimate default ('Der Accent ruht durchgängig auf der vorletzten Silbe'); the word-final heavy-diphthong case is stated only in Faria Junior 2022.

catalog_quote: No words in Bakairi differentiate their meaning through the variation of stress. Indeed, stress is predictable in Bakairi. With very few exceptions, the main stress occurs on the second to last mora as illustrated below. [ˈnɨkɨ] 'he slept', [nɨˈkɨmɔ] 'they slept' ... [ˈeɣɔ] 'pestle', [eˈɡɔɾɯ] 'his pestle', [eɡɔˈɾɯmɔ] 'their pestle(s)' ... In monosyllabic words, the nucleus is realized as a long vowel. If we define a lengthened vowel as containing two moras, it may be stated that the minimal word in Bakairi is bimoraic. ... Words with four or more syllables can exhibit secondary stress on the second syllable to the left of the main stressed syllable. ... Rising diphthongs, as in CV.(C)GV##, fail to attract stress to the word-final syllable. Consequently, words ending in a rising diphthong do not constitute complex rhymes, as the glide [j] or [w] belongs to the syllable onset. In contrast…

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, stress on the penultimate mora with CVG falling diphthongs heavy) rests on a 2022 reference grammar with a dedicated stress section, held locally, and every quoted sentence in the record (quote, the domain quotation, exception footnote, nasal-suffix clause) was found verbatim at the stated sections/pages (2.4.1 pp.45-46; 2.2 p.35-36 region; fn.13). The 1892 von den Steinen statement (penult default, final stress on diphthong-final words) is also confirmed in the scanned text we hold at p.320 and independently agrees. Glottolog's bibliography and a Crossref search show no newer or more specialised stress/prosody study; the one open phonology article found (Rosa & Bonfim 2020) was downloaded and is silent on stress placement; WALS has no stress coding for Bakairi. The two works still to obtain (Wheatley's SIL phonemics ms., Meira 2005) are corroborative only and low priority.

sources.quote: Stress generally occurs on the penultimate vowel. ['pařu] /pařu/ 'water' [u'gɔ̃ndɔ] /ugɔ̃dɔ/ 'man' ['təsι] /təsi̶/ 'he eats' [kadakɔbə'dιli] /kadakɔbədi̶li/ 'I am taking a walk' [wi'tai] /witai/ 'I bathed' [ədai'tuɔ] /ədaituɔ/ 'for what' [wi'tɔ̃ĩ] /witɔ̃ĩ/ 'for to bathe' [udəži'wau] /udəziwau/ 'I am going now'. If only one nasalized vowel occurs word final, the stress occurs on that vowel. [sapi'gũ] /sapigũ/ 'wet' [Eduka'pĩ̶] /Edukapĩ̶/ 'girl's name'. If the penultimate vowel is the second of a glide sequence (a sequence of two vowels in which the first vowel is lower than the second), the accent occurs on the antipenultimate rather than the penultimate vowel. ['kəedə] /kəedə/ 'I came' ['kɔ̃ĩndə] /kɔ̃ĩdə/ 'good' ['paitə] /paitə/ 'blanket' ['ñə̃ũndu] /yə̃ũdu/ 'his sister'

sources.note: Only other primary synchronic phonemic description of Bakairi (missionary fieldwork 1960s-80s, Eastern dialect); would give an independent pre-2022 stress statement to set beside Faria's mora analysis and von den Steinen 1892. Not expected to change the classification.
